script.title: Medicare fraud: free tests, free braces, and the card thieves want
script.hook: 5 Medicare scams target your parents' Medicare number. Here's each one, and how to read the statement that catches them.

segments.heading: Why your number
segments.narration: Your Medicare number is worth more to a scammer than your credit card. A card gets cancelled in a day. A Medicare number can be billed for tests, equipment and services for months before anyone notices, and the person it belongs to is often the last to find out. So the scams on this list all have one goal: get the number. Here are five of them, and the one habit that catches all five.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Free genetic tests
segments.narration: Scam one, the free genetic test. A caller, a table at a health fair, or someone at the door offers a cheek swab to check for cancer or heart risk, covered by Medicare. They need your Medicare number to send the kit. The test may never be read by anyone, but Medicare gets billed, and if your own doctor didn't order it and Medicare denies it, the bill can come back to you. The rule: only take a test your own doctor orders.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Free braces
segments.narration: Scam two, the free brace. Do you have back pain, knee pain, shoulder pain? Medicare will cover a brace at no cost. Then a box arrives with equipment nobody needed, sometimes several. Medicare pays for it, and your number goes on a list that gets sold to the next scammer. Medicare and your doctor don't cold-call to sell equipment.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The new card call
segments.narration: Scam three, the new card call. Medicare is issuing new cards, or your card has expired, just confirm your number. Medicare doesn't call you out of the blue for your number. If you need a replacement card, you get it through Medicare's own website or by calling 1-800-MEDICARE yourself.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Plan switch pressure
segments.narration: Scam four is pressure to switch plans, especially during enrollment periods. A caller says you qualify for extra benefits, a grocery card or more money back, if you switch today and confirm your details. Some are aggressive salespeople, some are scammers. Either way, don't decide on a cold call. Compare plans yourself on Medicare's site or with your State Health Insurance Assistance Program, which is free.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Fake fraud department
segments.narration: Scam five is the twist: someone calls from Medicare's fraud department, saying your number has been used in fraud and they need to verify it. They're the fraud. Real investigators don't need you to read your number to them.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Read the statement
segments.narration: Now the habit that catches all five. Every few months, Medicare sends a Medicare Summary Notice, or you can see the same thing in your online account. It lists every service and supply billed to your number. Go down the list with your parent. Any test you didn't have, any equipment that never came, any doctor you've never seen, is a red flag. It takes ten minutes, and it's the only way most people ever find out.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: If you spot fraud
segments.narration: If you spot something, call 1-800-MEDICARE and report it, or report it to the inspector general's hotline. Keep the statement. And remember the rule for every one of these calls: never give your Medicare number to anyone who contacted you. Your doctor already has it. Nobody else needs it on the phone.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: George and the health fair
segments.narration: Let's follow one made-up case to the statement. George, seventy-three, stops at a table at a community health fair. A friendly woman offers a free genetic cheek swab for cancer risk, covered by Medicare, and asks for his Medicare card to fill in the form. He hands it over. A few weeks later, a knee brace he never asked for arrives in the mail.
segments.on_screen_text: A free cheek swab, made up
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: an older man at a folding table at a health fair, a cheek swab kit and a clipboard. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The statement
segments.narration: When his Medicare Summary Notice comes, George reads it with his daughter, the way this video suggests. Two lines stand out: a genetic test billed for thousands of dollars, ordered by a doctor he's never met, and a knee brace from a supplier he's never heard of. His own doctor never ordered either.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a printed statement on a kitchen table with two lines highlighted, a magnifying glass. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: What they do
segments.narration: They call 1-800-MEDICARE, read out the two lines, and report it. They also report it to the inspector general's hotline and keep the statement and the brace box. George refuses any more deliveries, and from then on, his rule is simple: only a test or equipment his own doctor orders. His number was used, but catching it on the statement helps stop more billing in his name.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: an older man and his daughter on a call, a box marked return to sender. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Why the swab was the scam
segments.narration: Why does a free swab cost so much? Because the test isn't the product. George's Medicare number is. Once the scammers have it, they can bill Medicare for expensive tests and equipment in his name, often using a doctor who never saw him. If Medicare denies those claims because his own doctor didn't order them, a bill can even come back to him. So the free test is really a form to collect his number.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a Medicare-style card with a hook on it, a stack of bills behind. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The plan-switch call
segments.narration: A month later, in a different scam, a caller tells George he qualifies for a grocery allowance if he switches plans today, and he just needs to confirm his Medicare number. He says no, hangs up, and calls the number on his own plan card to ask. His plan says it didn't call. Two scams, one rule: nobody who calls him first gets his Medicare number.

script.title: Graduates' guide: fake jobs, fake landlords and scholarship scams
script.hook: 6 scams target new graduates in their first summer. Here's each one, and a 10-minute setup before the first paycheck.

segments.heading: Why grads
segments.narration: Your first summer after graduation is a scammer's favourite season. You're applying for jobs, looking for an apartment, and handling money on your own, often for the first time. Scammers know exactly what you're searching for. Here are six scams aimed right at you, and a ten-minute setup that protects you.

segments.heading: The chat interview
segments.narration: Scam one, the chat-app interview. A recruiter finds you, the interview happens entirely by text on Telegram, WhatsApp or Signal, and you're hired within hours. Real employers interview on video or in person. Look the company up yourself, and email the recruiter at the company's real domain.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The equipment check
segments.narration: Scam two follows straight on: the equipment check. Your new employer sends a check to buy a laptop from their approved vendor. You deposit it, pay the vendor, and days later the check bounces. The bank takes the money back. What you sent the vendor is gone. Real employers never send you money to buy their equipment.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Onboarding identity theft
segments.narration: Scam three, early paperwork. They want your Social Security number, a photo of your license and your bank details for direct deposit before you've seen an offer letter or met anyone. That's identity theft. Real onboarding comes after a real offer, through a real HR system.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Scholarship fees
segments.narration: Scam four, scholarship and aid fees. You've won a scholarship you never applied for, just pay a processing fee. Or a service charges to file your FAFSA. Real scholarships don't charge, and the FAFSA is free. Your school's financial aid office will help for nothing.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The apartment
segments.narration: Scam five, the apartment that can't be shown. Great rent, copied photos, a landlord who's out of the country, and a deposit by payment app to hold it. People have reported sixty-five million dollars lost to rental scams. Never pay before you, or someone you trust, has been inside.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Maya's first summer
segments.narration: Let's follow one made-up graduate through her first summer, because these scams often come together. Maya finishes college in May. In one June week she gets a chat-app job offer for a remote data role, an email saying she's won a scholarship for grad school she never applied for, and finds an apartment listing in her new city that's three hundred dollars under everything else.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a young woman in a cap and gown photo on a shelf, a laptop with three message windows. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The job
segments.narration: The job comes first. A recruiter interviews her entirely by text and offers the role two hours later, at a salary well above what her classmates are getting. The next day, onboarding asks for her Social Security number, a photo of her driver's license, and her bank login 'to set up direct deposit'. A real employer asks for tax forms after a real offer, and never for a bank login. She checks the company's own careers page, typed in herself: no such role.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a chat window showing a fast job offer, a careers page with no matching listing. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The scholarship and the apartment
segments.narration: The scholarship wants a ninety-five dollar processing fee. Real scholarships don't make you pay to receive them, so she deletes it. The apartment landlord is out of the country and wants a deposit by payment app before she can see it. She asks a friend in that city to visit the address. The friend finds people already living there, who've never heard of the listing.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a fee request email crossed out, a friend standing outside an apartment door holding a phone. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: What she did right
segments.narration: What made Maya hard to scam wasn't knowing every trick. Before the search started she froze her credit, turned on bank alerts, and set one rule for the summer: no money and no ID numbers to anyone she hasn't verified on her own. Three scams in one week, zero dollars lost. And she signed up for the real job fair her college career office runs every July.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a young woman with a checklist on a phone, a padlock icon and a calendar with a job fair circled. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: If she'd sent the ID
segments.narration: And if she had already sent her Social Security number and license photo? The same day: freeze credit at all three bureaus if it isn't already, report it at IdentityTheft dot gov for a recovery plan, watch bank and card alerts closely, and consider an IRS Identity Protection PIN so nobody can file a return with her number. It's fixable, and faster is better.

The tell is the same as the scholarship fee: paying to get money that's supposed to be free.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a laptop showing a paid form service crossed out next to a free official form. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Her 10-minute setup
segments.narration: Here's exactly what Maya did in May, in ten minutes. Credit freezes at Equifax, Experian and TransUnion, free. Transaction alerts on her bank and card. A unique password and two-step sign-in on her email, because email resets everything else. And a note in her phone: no money and no ID numbers to anyone I haven't verified myself. That note is what she read when the job offer came.

segments.narration: Now the setup. Freeze your credit at Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. It's free. Turn on alerts for every bank and card transaction. Put a strong, unique password and two-step sign-in on your email. And make one rule: you never pay to get a job, an apartment or a scholarship. That rule alone beats most of this list.

script.title: Veterans' benefit scams and fake military charities: what to know before Memorial Day
script.hook: 4 scams target veterans and the people who want to help them. Here's each one, and who to trust for free help.

segments.heading: Why veterans
segments.narration: Veterans and military families are targeted for the same reasons they're respected: steady benefits, a strong sense of duty, and a public that wants to help. Scammers use all three. Here are four scams to know before Memorial Day, and where to get real help for free.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Pension poaching
segments.narration: Scam one, pension poaching. It often starts with a free lunch seminar or a friendly adviser who promises to get an older veteran, or a surviving spouse, a bigger VA pension fast. Then come fees to fill in forms, and advice to move savings into annuities or trusts. Moving assets can tie up money the family needs and can affect eligibility for other help, like Medicaid. VA warns about exactly this.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Free help
segments.narration: The answer is simple. Help applying for VA benefits is available for free from VA-accredited representatives, including veterans service organizations. Anyone can check a helper's name on VA's accreditation search. If they're not listed, or they're charging to file a first claim, or selling an investment, walk away.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Impostor VA calls
segments.narration: Scam two, the impostor VA call. Your benefits are on hold, or you're owed back pay, just confirm your Social Security number and bank account. VA doesn't call to ask for that. Hang up and contact VA on the number from its own website.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Fake charities
segments.narration: Scam three, the fake veterans' charity. Calls spike before Memorial Day and Veterans Day. The name sounds like a big, real charity. The caller wants a pledge tonight, sometimes by gift card. Look the charity up yourself, check it with a watchdog, and give on its own site. Ask how much reaches veterans; a real charity can tell you.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Fake soldiers
segments.narration: Scam four aims at everyone else: the fake soldier. Stolen photos of a real service member, a profile on a dating app, a deployment that means no video calls, and then a need for money: leave, a flight home, a package fee. Real service members don't pay for their leave. Never send money to someone you haven't met.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Your checklist
segments.narration: Your checklist. One, VA help is free from accredited representatives. Two, never move savings because someone promised more pension. Three, VA won't call for your numbers. Four, check a charity before you give. Five, never send money to an online love interest you haven't met.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: If it happened
segments.narration: If a veteran in your family already paid a pension poacher or gave out their details, contact VA, report it to the VA inspector general, and report it to the FTC at report fraud dot f t c dot gov. And thank you, to everyone who served, and everyone who looks out for them.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Frank's lunch seminar
segments.narration: Let's follow one made-up case. Frank is eighty-two and served two tours. He gets an invitation to a free lunch seminar on veterans' benefits at a local restaurant. The speaker is warm, calls everyone sir, and says many veterans are missing out on a pension they qualify for. Afterwards he offers Frank a private meeting to 'restructure' his savings so he'll qualify.
segments.on_screen_text: A free lunch and a promise
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: an older veteran at a restaurant table with a free lunch, a speaker with a slideshow. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The pitch
segments.narration: At the meeting, the adviser says Frank's savings are too high for the pension, so he should move them into an annuity the adviser sells, and the adviser's firm will file the VA claim for a fee. It sounds like help. But moving savings this way can lock up the money for years, may not make him eligible, and can even affect other benefits he relies on.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a document with a pen and a dotted signature line, a pie chart of savings being moved. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Free help instead
segments.narration: Frank's daughter looks up VA's accreditation search together with him. The adviser isn't accredited. They find a veterans service organization nearby with an accredited representative, who reviews his situation for free. Frank doesn't qualify for that pension, and moving his savings wouldn't have changed it in a way that helped him. He'd have paid fees and lost access to his own money for nothing.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a veteran and his daughter meeting a friendly representative at an office desk. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The Memorial Day call
segments.narration: Two weeks later, before Memorial Day, a caller asks Frank for a pledge to a veterans' charity with a name close to a big one he's heard of. He says he only gives to charities he looks up himself, and he gives on the charity's own website instead. The caller pushes, then hangs up. That push is the tell. Real charities are happy for you to check and give later.

segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: an older man on a landline shaking his head politely, a laptop showing a charity website. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: If he'd signed
segments.narration: If Frank had signed and paid, the steps are: contact VA about the claim, report the adviser to the VA inspector general and to his state's attorney general, report it at ReportFraud dot FTC dot gov, and talk to an accredited representative about what can still be undone. segments.heading: The fake soldier
segments.narration: The same summer, Frank's granddaughter matches with 'Sergeant Mike' on a dating app. He's deployed, can't video call, and after a month needs four hundred dollars for a leave request so he can come home to meet her. Frank tells her what the VA and the Army say: service members don't pay for leave, and real soldiers can talk to family. She does a reverse image search; the photos belong to a real soldier with a different name.

script.title: The summer travel scam guide: flights, bookings, rentals and road trips
script.hook: 5 travel scams peak in June. Here's each one, from the fake airline text to the gas pump skimmer.

segments.heading: Why summer
segments.narration: Summer travel means booking under pressure, delays you can't control, and lots of card payments on the road. That's the perfect setup for five scams. Here's each one, and the habits that beat all of them.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Flight canceled texts
segments.narration: Scam one, the canceled flight text. Your flight has been canceled, call this number to rebook. The agent charges a rebooking fee, takes your card, and your new ticket never appears. Scammers also buy search ads for airline help lines and reply to people complaining on social media. Get help only through the airline's app, or the number on your booking confirmation.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Lookalike booking sites
segments.narration: Scam two, the lookalike booking site. A search ad that looks like the hotel's official site, with the same photos and a great price. You get a confirmation the hotel has never heard of, or fees that double the price. Type the hotel's address yourself, then call the hotel to confirm your booking.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Fake rentals
segments.narration: Scam three, the vacation rental that doesn't exist. Photos copied from a real listing, a host who wants you off the platform to save on fees, and payment by wire or payment app. Search the photos and the address, keep every message and payment on the platform, and pay by credit card.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Skimmers
segments.narration: Scam four, skimmers. At the gas pump or an ATM, a hidden device copies your card. Wiggle the reader, check the pump's security seal, choose pumps near the store, use ATMs inside banks, and best of all, tap to pay. Use a credit card, not debit, on the road.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Free trip offers
segments.narration: Scam five, the free trip. You've won a cruise or a vacation, just pay taxes and port fees, or sit through a pitch. Real prizes don't make you pay to collect them.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Your checklist
segments.narration: Your summer travel checklist. Type travel sites yourself. Read the web address before you pay. Pay by credit card. Stay on the booking platform. Get airline numbers from the app. Tap to pay at the pump. And turn on card alerts before you leave.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: If it happened
segments.narration: If you paid a fake agent or a fake host, call your card company the same day and dispute the charge, then report it to the FTC at report fraud dot f t c dot gov. Then go and enjoy your summer.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The Lee family road trip
segments.narration: Let's follow one made-up road trip from booking to home. In May, the Lees search for a lake hotel, and the first result is an ad with the hotel's photos and a rate eighty dollars lower than everywhere else. They check the web address before paying and it's a booking site with a similar name, not the hotel. They close it and book on the hotel's own site, on a credit card.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a family at a laptop with a lake hotel photo, a web address with a highlighted wrong letter. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Day 2: the pump
segments.narration: On the drive, at a quiet gas station off the highway, Mr. Lee wiggles the card reader, the way this video shows. It shifts and the pump's security seal looks broken. He drives to a pump nearer the store, taps his card instead of swiping, and mentions the loose reader to the cashier.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a hand gently testing a card reader at a gas pump, a broken seal sticker. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Day 4: the cancelled flight
segments.narration: Mrs. Lee's mother is flying in to join them. A text says her flight is cancelled and gives a number to rebook. Her mother calls Mrs. Lee first instead, because that's the family rule. They open the airline's app together. The flight is on time. The number in the text wasn't the airline's.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: an older woman at an airport gate calling her daughter, an airline app showing on time. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Day 6: the prize
segments.narration: On the last day, a call says the family won a free cruise from a survey they took at a rest stop. They just need to pay two hundred forty-nine dollars in port fees. Their twelve-year-old says, 'You don't pay for a prize.' They hang up. Four scams in six days, and the whole defense was the checklist: type the address, check the pump, get numbers from the app, and never pay to collect a prize.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a family in a car laughing, a phone on speaker with a cruise ship icon crossed out. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: What it could have cost
segments.narration: Add it up. The lookalike booking site might have taken around six hundred dollars with no room at the end. A skimmer could have copied a card for fraud charges. The fake rebooking line often charges a few hundred dollars and takes a booking code. The cruise prize, two hundred forty-nine. Not one of those needed expert knowledge to stop. They needed a habit, and a family that uses it.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a jar labelled saved with a few bills, a car parked by a lake at sunset. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The rental they didn't book
segments.narration: Before they settled on the hotel, the Lees had found a lake cabin for half the going rate. The host replied in minutes and asked them to pay by wire to skip platform fees. They searched the photos and found the same cabin on the real platform, under a different host, at the normal price. They reported the fake listing. Rule of thumb: stay on the platform, pay on the platform, and use a credit card.
segments.on_screen_text: A lake cabin at half price
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a lake cabin photo duplicated with two different prices, one crossed out. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: If it had happened
segments.narration: And if one had slipped through? Call the card company the same day and dispute the charge. Report it at ReportFraud dot FTC dot gov. If you gave a booking code to a fake agent, check the booking in the airline's app. If you typed a password into a lookalike site, change it, and the same password anywhere else. Most travel scams are recoverable only if you move fast.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a phone call to a card company, a checklist with three items, a suitcase. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The checks

segments.heading: Answer
segments.narration: Tapping to pay, because a tap doesn't share the data a skimmer copies. Credit over debit is next: if your card is copied, the money missing isn't from your checking account while the bank sorts it out.

segments.heading: Card alerts
segments.narration: And turn on card alerts before you leave. If a skimmed card gets used, you'll see the charge in minutes, not at the end of the month, and you can lock the card from the app while you're still on the road.

segments.heading: Pay smart
